summary:
North Kalimantan stands under the national framework of Indonesia, and no trans-specific safety finding is recorded for the province itself. It is assessed at the national score: a trans visitor in North Kalimantan faces the legal and physical risks carried by Indonesia as a whole.

Indonesia's penal code, signed in December 2022, took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual sex between unmarried adults with up to one year's imprisonment. Because same-sex marriage is not recognised, the provision reaches all consensual same-sex relations; reporting indicates prosecutions are selective rather than systematic.

Official hostility is now written into national policy. An October 2025 presidential decree lists 'the promotion of LGBTQ+ culture' among nonmilitary threats, alongside terrorism and drug addiction. In July 2026 mobs attacked transgender women in several cities, including West Java, and no prosecutions of the attackers have been reported. Reporting dated 14 August 2026 records civil society assessments that conditions are rapidly worsening.

Protections are absent on paper. Indonesia has no anti-discrimination or hate-crime provisions based on sexual orientation or gender identity, no national law shielding a visitor or resident from harassment on those grounds, and no legal recognition of same-sex partnerships. Legal gender recognition requires sex-reassignment surgery and a judge's approval, and only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors are available on Indonesian documents.

Provincial religious law adds a harder layer in one part of the country. Same-sex sexual activity is illegal in Aceh under Sharia, punishable by flogging or imprisonment, and those penalties apply to anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors. A proposed obscenity article explicitly naming 'same sex' is feared to trigger discriminatory regional bylaws, which would extend such reach to provinces including North Kalimantan.

Physical risk falls hardest on visibly gender-nonconforming people. Vigilante mobs attack transgender people with impunity, and the July 2026 assaults proceeded without prosecution. A trans traveller has also died in Indonesian custody: in August 2022 Rodrigo Ventocilla, a Harvard student on honeymoon in Bali, was arrested at an airport on drug charges and died in detention, with his mother alleging police beat him and police denying violence was used.

Expression is criminalised in ways a visitor can trigger. The 2006 Law Against Pornography and Pornoaction punishes writing or audio-visual material showing or suggesting same-sex relations with up to seven years' imprisonment, the national broadcasting commission banned presenting LGBTQ behaviour as normal on television and radio in March 2016, and the government has blocked websites and apps carrying 'gay' or LGBTQ-related terms, including Grindr. A bill to prohibit online content presenting lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender behaviour was under discussion in 2025.
tangentialFactors:
Public opinion forms part of the environment a visitor enters. A 2025 Pew Research Center figure put 93% of Indonesians calling homosexuality 'morally unacceptable', a level of social disapproval that underlies both mob action and the absence of prosecutions against it.

Indonesia has voted against the United Nations independent expert on sexual orientation and gender identity, positioning the government against the international protection machinery a visitor might otherwise invoke.

Conversion therapy is widely practised and openly advertised, including in provinces with no trans-specific findings of their own. This indicates organised domestic capacity to act against LGBT people that a visitor may encounter in practice even where no local legal case is recorded.

Aceh is the clearest illustration of the sub-national layer: its Sharia punishments reach foreigners directly. North Kalimantan has no equivalent provision recorded, and the risks here are those of the national regime rather than of a provincial religious code.

outOfScopeNotes:
Two figures circulate for the same penal-code provision: the national framework records up to two years' imprisonment for consensual extra-marital sex, while the source used for this pass records up to one year. The discrepancy is unresolved here.

No source in this inventory reports prosecutions, police raids, vigilante incidents or regional bylaws within North Kalimantan itself. The province's risk assessment rests entirely on national-level material.

The status and passage date of the proposed obscenity article naming 'same sex', and of the 2025 bill on online LGBT content, are not resolved in the sources provided; whether either has been enacted, and whether North Kalimantan has adopted or considered any regional bylaw under it, is not sourced.

The number of cities affected by the July 2026 mob attacks, beyond West Java, is not specified in the inventory, and no figures for injuries or arrests are available.
